Overlap the hard-tool build with bridge production so deliveries do not pause, and plan the cutover so the first hard-tool parts are qualified before the bridge tool retires.

steps.description: Make the hard-tooling investment decision on a frozen design: breakeven volume, payback, tool life, and the risk of committing non-recurring cost.

inputs.name: low-rate-production-plan
inputs.desc: The low-rate production results and the demonstrated demand and design stability

inputs.name: volume-forecast
inputs.desc: The forecast production volume, rate, and program life over which the hard tool amortizes

outputs.name: investment-decision
outputs.desc: The go/no-go on hard tooling with the breakeven volume, payback period, and the unit-cost and rate gains quantified

outputs.name: hard-tool-specification
outputs.desc: The hard-tool specification: material, cavity count, expected life, and the rate and tolerance it must deliver

process: Compute the breakeven volume between bridge and hard tooling. Breakeven is the non-recurring hard-tool cost divided by the per-part saving over bridge tooling; below that volume the bridge tool is cheaper overall, above it the hard tool wins. Compare the breakeven to the forecast volume with margin for forecast error.

Require a frozen design before committing. Hard tooling is the point of no cheap return: a design change after a hardened-steel multi-cavity tool is cut is expensive and slow. Confirm the design is frozen under change control and the qualification is complete or nearly so before releasing the hard-tool cut.

Specify the tool for the rate and life, not just the part. Set the cavity count from the production rate and cycle time, the tool material (hardened tool steel for millions of cycles, with appropriate coatings and cooling) from the total volume and material abrasiveness, and the cooling and ejection design from the cycle time the rate demands. The tool is a production-rate decision as much as a part decision.

Quantify the unit-cost and rate gains that justify the spend. Hard tooling lowers per-part cost (multi-cavity, fast cycle, low scrap) and raises sustainable rate; put numbers on both and show the payback period against the forecast. An investment justified only by 'we will need it eventually' without a volume and payback is not justified.

Weigh the downside of committing early against waiting. Committing hard tooling too early risks an expensive change if the design or volume shifts; waiting too long leaves the program on costly bridge tooling and capped rate. State the risk on each side and the trigger conditions, so the decision is made on evidence rather than hope about the forecast.

description: Manage mass properties across a hardware program from mass budget and allocation through tracking and growth reporting to center-of-gravity and inertia estimation and mass-reduction trades, so weight is controlled rather than discovered at integration.

steps.description: Set the total mass target and allocate it top-down to subsystems with maturity-based margins and not-to-exceed limits.

inputs.name: mass-requirement
inputs.desc: The system-level mass target or limit (for example maximum launch mass, payload capacity) and its source

inputs.name: system-architecture
inputs.desc: The subsystem breakdown the mass must be allocated across

outputs.name: mass-allocation
outputs.desc: The mass budget allocated to each subsystem, with a not-to-exceed value and a target value for each

outputs.name: margin-plan
outputs.desc: The mass growth allowance and management reserve held at each level and how they shrink as the design matures

process: Start from the hard system limit and work down. Identify the physical limit (launch vehicle capacity, structural rating, range requirement) and set the system mass target below it with a management reserve. Allocate the remainder to subsystems by function and by historical mass fraction for similar systems, so the allocation is grounded in data, not wishful splitting.

Hold a mass growth allowance sized to the design maturity. Early-stage estimates grow; carry a growth allowance that is large at concept (often 20 to 30% at the system level for a new design) and shrinks as mass moves from estimated to calculated to measured. The allowance is a planned reserve to be consumed deliberately, not slack to be spent silently.

Give each subsystem both a target and a not-to-exceed value. The target is what the subsystem designs to; the not-to-exceed is the allocation it may not cross without a system-level trade. The gap between them is the margin the system holds against that subsystem's growth.

Allocate to the controlling party and make it accountable. Each subsystem allocation has an owner who manages to it; a budget with no owner is not managed. Set the reporting cadence and the escalation path for an allocation that is trending over its not-to-exceed value.

Hold system-level management reserve separate from subsystem margins. Keep a reserve at the system level that only the system owner can release, so a subsystem overrun that cannot be recovered locally has a controlled path to resolution rather than silently eating the system margin. Document the reserve and the rules for drawing it down.

steps.description: Track actual mass bottom-up against the budget with basis-of-estimate codes and report growth trends so overruns surface early.

inputs.name: mass-allocation
inputs.desc: The subsystem mass budgets with target and not-to-exceed values

inputs.name: component-masses
inputs.desc: The current component mass values with their source: estimated, calculated, or measured

outputs.name: mass-status
outputs.desc: The current rolled-up mass against budget at system and subsystem level, with margin remaining and trend

outputs.name: growth-trend
outputs.desc: The mass-versus-time history and the projected mass at delivery, flagging subsystems trending over their not-to-exceed limit

process: Roll mass up bottom-up from a controlled component list. Every component carries a mass value and a basis code: measured (weighed hardware), calculated (from the detailed model), estimated (parametric or analogy), or allocated (a placeholder holding the budget). The rollup against the allocation shows margin remaining at each level.

Weight the margin by the basis maturity. A subsystem mostly on measured masses needs little remaining margin; one mostly on estimates needs more because it will still grow. Report not just the current mass but the quality of the number, so the system owner knows how much growth is still coming.

Track mass versus time and project to delivery. Plot the rolled-up mass across the program; a steadily rising line projects to a delivery mass that can be extrapolated well before integration. The trend, not just the snapshot, is what gives time to act on an overrun.

Flag and escalate subsystems trending over their not-to-exceed value. The reporting exists to surface a problem while it is still cheap to fix; a subsystem whose projection crosses its not-to-exceed limit triggers escalation to a trade study, not a note in a report nobody acts on. Set the threshold that triggers action.

Keep the mass record under configuration control and reconcile it with measured hardware. As components are built and weighed, replace estimates with measured values and reconcile the model; a large gap between calculated and measured mass is itself a finding (a process or model error) worth investigating. Maintain one controlled source of truth for mass.

steps.description: Estimate and control the center of gravity and the inertia tensor across configurations, and plan the measurement that confirms them.

inputs.name: mass-status
inputs.desc: The component mass list with positions for the current configuration

inputs.name: cg-requirements
inputs.desc: The allowable center-of-gravity envelope and the inertia limits the system must meet across its configurations

outputs.name: cg-inertia-estimate
outputs.desc: The estimated center of gravity and inertia tensor per configuration, against the allowable envelope and limits

outputs.name: measurement-plan
outputs.desc: The plan to measure mass, center of gravity, and inertia on the built hardware and reconcile to the estimate

process: Compute the center of gravity as the mass-weighted mean position of every component. Sum mass times position over total mass in each axis; carry it per configuration because the center of gravity moves as fuel burns, payloads change, or appendages deploy. Report the center-of-gravity travel across the full configuration set, not just one point.

Build the inertia tensor about the center of gravity. Sum each component's own inertia plus its mass times the squared offset from the system center of gravity (the parallel-axis theorem); report the full tensor including products of inertia, because a nonzero product of inertia causes cross-axis coupling that control and dynamics care about.

Check the center of gravity and inertia against the allowable envelope for every configuration. Stability, control authority, handling, and dynamic behavior all depend on where the center of gravity sits and how the inertia is distributed; a center of gravity that leaves its envelope in one configuration is a system problem even if it is fine in others. Flag the worst-case configuration.

Hold margin on the center-of-gravity estimate for the same reason as mass. The center of gravity is computed from component masses and positions that are still maturing, so the estimate has uncertainty; keep the predicted center of gravity comfortably inside the envelope early, and tighten as masses become measured.

Plan the physical measurement to confirm the estimate. Mass is weighed; center of gravity is found by multi-point weighing or a balance method; inertia is measured by a bifilar or torsional pendulum (period gives inertia) or a spin-balance machine. Plan these measurements on the built article and reconcile them to the estimate, because a model error in position shows up here and nowhere earlier.

steps.description: When mass exceeds budget, run a structured trade study to find the cheapest mass to remove using a cost-of-weight metric and the right methods.

inputs.name: growth-trend
inputs.desc: The overrun and the subsystems trending over their not-to-exceed limit

inputs.name: cg-inertia-estimate
inputs.desc: The current mass distribution and the center-of-gravity and inertia effects any change will have

outputs.name: reduction-options
outputs.desc: The ranked mass-reduction options with the mass saved, the cost and risk of each, and the center-of-gravity effect

outputs.name: recommended-actions
outputs.desc: The selected set of reductions that recover the budget at acceptable cost and risk, with the net mass and center-of-gravity result

process: Set the value of removing mass with a cost-of-weight metric. A program has an implied or explicit price per kilogram removed (often high for launch, aerospace, or range-limited systems); the metric tells you how much cost and risk a kilogram of saving justifies, so trades are decided on value, not on which engineer argues hardest.

Find the mass concentrations first. Most mass sits in a few places; a rank-ordered mass list (heaviest components and subsystems first) shows where a given percentage reduction yields the most kilograms. Chasing grams off a hundred small parts rarely beats redesigning the few heavy ones.

List the reduction methods against their cost and risk. Options run from low-risk (remove unused margin, thin lightly-loaded regions) through moderate (material substitution to higher specific-strength alloys or composites, topology optimization of structural parts) to high-risk (reducing a safety margin, deleting redundancy). Rank by mass saved per unit cost and by the risk each carries.

Check each option's effect on center of gravity and inertia, not just mass. Removing mass from one end moves the center of gravity and can push it out of its envelope even while reducing total mass; a mass reduction that violates the center-of-gravity requirement is not a valid option. Carry the center-of-gravity and inertia effect through the trade.

Select the set that recovers the budget at the lowest cost and risk, and re-check the system. Pick the combination of reductions that gets back inside the budget with margin, confirm the net center of gravity and inertia still meet their limits, and route the changes through configuration control. Record the options not taken so the next overrun does not re-study them.

description: Run hardware configuration management from drawing and document control through engineering change management to as-designed-versus-as-built tracking and effectivity and serialization, so the team always knows exactly what was designed, released, and built.

steps.description: Establish drawing and document control: the drawing tree, release states, revision scheme, and the single controlled source of released definition.

inputs.name: product-definition
inputs.desc: The drawings, models, specifications, and documents that define the product

inputs.name: release-process
inputs.desc: The review, approval, and release workflow the organization uses for controlled documents

outputs.name: drawing-tree
outputs.desc: The structured drawing tree and document index, from top assembly down to piece parts, with each item's current released revision

outputs.name: control-scheme
outputs.desc: The release-state and revision scheme: how documents move from draft to released, how revisions are identified, and where the controlled master lives

process: Build the drawing tree from the top assembly down to piece parts and specifications. The tree is the backbone of configuration management: it shows every item that makes up the product, its part number, and its current released revision, and it is how a change is traced to everything it affects. Keep one authoritative tree, not scattered lists.

Define the release states and the gate between them. A document is draft (in work, freely editable), in review (frozen for approval), or released (controlled, changeable only by a formal change). The gate from review to released is where the approvals are captured; a 'released' document that someone can edit directly is not under control.

Set an unambiguous part-number and revision scheme. Decide whether form-fit-function changes get a new part number versus a revision, and whether revisions are letters or numbers; a revision changes the definition of the same part number while a new part number means a part not interchangeable with the old. Interchangeability is the rule that decides which applies.

Keep a single controlled master and prevent uncontrolled copies. The released definition lives in one controlled repository (a product data management system), and working copies are clearly marked uncontrolled. The most common configuration failure is someone building to an out-of-date printout; control is only real if people cannot easily use the wrong revision.

Make the current released revision of every item visible to everyone who needs it. Engineering, manufacturing, procurement, and quality must all see the same current revision; a change is only effective when everyone downstream is working to it. Define how the released state and current revision are published and how obsolete revisions are withdrawn.

steps.description: Run the change process: change request, classification, impact assessment, approval, and the change order that releases the new definition.

inputs.name: drawing-tree
inputs.desc: The released definition and the items a change would affect

inputs.name: change-need
inputs.desc: The reason for the change: a defect, an improvement, a cost reduction, or a requirement change

outputs.name: change-package
outputs.desc: The change request, its classification, the impact assessment across affected items, and the approved change order

outputs.name: disposition-plan
outputs.desc: The disposition of affected in-process and fielded units (use-as-is, rework, scrap, retrofit) and the effectivity point for the change

process: Start every change as a request that states the problem, not the solution. The change request (ECR) captures why a change is needed and what it must achieve; separating the request from the implementing order keeps a record of the problem and prevents a half-analyzed fix from being released. Route the request to a change board for a decision to pursue it.

Classify the change by its impact on form, fit, function, and interface. A major change (Class I) affects form, fit, function, interface, interchangeability, safety, or a controlled requirement and needs full review and often customer approval; a minor change (Class II) is a documentation or non-interchangeable-detail fix. The classification sets the approval level and the rigor.

Assess impact across everything the drawing tree connects. A change ripples to mating parts, interfaces, tooling, test procedures, spares, manuals, and qualification; use the drawing tree to find every affected item and assess each. The commonest change failure is updating the part but not the tooling, the test, or the mating part.

Release the change through a controlled change order (ECN/ECO). After approval, the change order formally supersedes the old revision with the new, records the approvals, and is the authority for everyone downstream to switch. The order names the effectivity point so manufacturing knows exactly which units get the change.

Disposition the units already in process and in the field. Decide for each affected population: use-as-is (the change is an improvement, old units are acceptable), rework, scrap, or retrofit. A safety change may force retrofit of fielded units; an improvement may apply only to new production. Record the disposition and the effectivity so the as-built record stays accurate.

steps.description: Track the as-built configuration against the as-designed definition, capturing deviations and waivers so each unit's true configuration is known.

inputs.name: change-package
inputs.desc: The released definition and change history that defines the as-designed configuration

inputs.name: build-records
inputs.desc: The manufacturing records of what was actually built on each unit: parts installed, revisions, and any departures

outputs.name: as-built-record
outputs.desc: The per-unit as-built configuration: the part numbers and revisions actually installed, against the as-designed baseline

outputs.name: deviation-log
outputs.desc: The authorized deviations and waivers on each unit, with the nonconformance, the disposition, and the approval

process: Baseline the as-designed configuration for each unit's effectivity. The as-designed configuration is the set of released part numbers and revisions that a given unit is supposed to have, driven by the effectivity point from the change orders. Establish it before the build so there is a defined expectation to build against and check.

Record the as-built configuration as the unit is built, not after. Capture the actual part number and revision of every item installed, the lot or serial of traceable parts, and the operator and date. An as-built record reconstructed from memory after delivery is unreliable; it must be captured at the point of installation.

Document every departure as an authorized deviation or waiver. A deviation is a pre-build authorization to depart from the definition for specific units; a waiver accepts a nonconformance found after the fact. Each needs the nonconformance described, the engineering disposition (use-as-is with rationale, rework, scrap), and the approval. Undocumented departures destroy configuration integrity.

Reconcile as-built against as-designed and resolve every gap. Compare the as-built record to the as-designed baseline for each unit; every difference is either a documented deviation/waiver or an escape to be investigated. The reconciliation is what makes the as-built record trustworthy, not just present.

Keep the per-unit record retrievable for the life of the unit. Field support, failure investigation, and retrofit all need to know a specific unit's true configuration years later. Store the as-built and deviation records against the unit serial so the exact configuration of any delivered unit can be recovered on demand.

steps.description: Define effectivity and serialization so each change applies to an exactly known set of units and each unit is individually traceable.

inputs.name: as-built-record
inputs.desc: The per-unit configuration and the units in and out of production

inputs.name: traceability-requirements
inputs.desc: The level of traceability the product requires: serial, lot, or batch, driven by safety, regulatory, or warranty needs

outputs.name: effectivity-scheme
outputs.desc: How effectivity is expressed and applied: by serial number, block, date, or lot, so each change has a precise cut-in point

outputs.name: serialization-plan
outputs.desc: The serialization and marking plan: which items are serialized, how they are marked, and how the as-built record links to each serial

process: Choose how effectivity is expressed to match the product. Effectivity can be by serial number (unit 101 and up), by block or lot, or by date; serial-number effectivity gives the most precise cut-in and is standard for complex, safety-relevant, or low-rate hardware, while lot or date effectivity suits high-rate commodity parts. Every change order states its effectivity in this scheme.

Make every change's cut-in point unambiguous. A change that is 'effective soon' creates built-wrong units in the gap; the effectivity names the exact first unit (or lot, or date) that gets the change and confirms the disposition of everything before it. Manufacturing builds to the effectivity, so it must be precise.

Decide which items are serialized and to what depth. Serialize items that need individual life tracking, failure traceability, or warranty and regulatory tracking (structural parts, life-limited parts, safety-critical assemblies); lot-trace fasteners and raw material; batch-track consumables. Over-serializing wastes effort, under-serializing loses the traceability a failure investigation needs.

Mark serials durably and link them to the as-built record. Apply the serial by a method that survives the part's service life (laser etch, data-matrix, stamped plate) and tie that serial to the unit's as-built configuration, so scanning or reading the serial retrieves exactly what that unit is and what changes apply to it. A serial that does not link to a record is just a number.

Maintain the where-used and effectivity links both ways. From a change, you must find every effective unit; from a unit's serial, you must find its full configuration and every change applied to it. Keep the forward (change-to-units) and reverse (unit-to-configuration) links current so recalls, retrofits, and investigations can resolve the exact affected population.
